intro: Lingashtakam is a short Sanskrit stotra of eight verses in praise of the Shiva linga, the form in which Shiva is worshipped in most temples across India. The text is traditional, and its author is not recorded by name, which is common for stotras that have been carried through oral and temple recitation for generations rather than through a single attributed composition. Lingashtakam moves through a set of qualities and episodes associated with the linga - its purity, its fragrance when anointed, the stories connected with it, and the devotion of gods and sages toward it - closing each verse with the same line of salutation to Sadashiva. A final couplet after the eight verses states what the tradition holds about reciting it. People encounter Lingashtakam most often in the context of daily or festival worship of Shiva, recited either privately or as part of group chanting at a temple, particularly where a Shiva linga is the central deity.

groups.heading: Verse 1 - Purity and the end of the sorrow of birth
groups.body: The opening verse of Lingashtakam describes the linga as worshipped by Brahma, Vishnu (called Murari) and the gods, and as shining with a stainless, radiant quality. It then names the linga as that which destroys the sorrow born of birth - a reference to the cycle of birth and the suffering associated with worldly existence. The verse ends with the refrain that recurs through the whole text: a bowing down to the Sadashiva linga. This opening sets the pattern the rest of Lingashtakam follows - a few descriptive lines building toward the same closing salutation.

groups.heading: Verse 2 - Honoured by sages, connected to the Kama and Ravana episodes
groups.body: The second verse of Lingashtakam speaks of the linga as worshipped by the best among gods and sages, and as compassionate in nature. It refers to the linga in connection with the burning of Kama, the god of desire, a well-known episode in Shiva's mythology, and with the humbling of Ravana's pride, another familiar story where Shiva's power checks Ravana's arrogance. These are brief mythological references rather than retellings - the verse simply places the linga at the centre of both episodes before returning to the closing line of salutation.

groups.heading: Verse 3 - Fragrance, wisdom, and the devotion of accomplished beings
groups.body: Here Lingashtakam describes the linga as anointed with all manner of fragrances, evoking the ritual practice of applying sandal paste and other scented substances during worship. The verse also calls the linga a cause of the growth of intellect or discernment, linking devotion to the linga with clarity of mind. It notes that the linga is honoured by the Siddhas - accomplished beings - as well as by gods and asuras alike, suggesting a form of reverence that crosses the usual divide between these groups.

groups.heading: Verse 4 - Adornment and the Daksha yajna episode
groups.body: This verse of Lingashtakam describes the linga as adorned with gold and great jewels, and as encircled and made beautiful by the serpent lord - a reference to the serpent Shiva wears. It then mentions the destruction of Daksha's sacrifice, another well-known story in which Shiva's intervention disrupts a yajna conducted without due honour to him. As with the Ravana reference earlier, this is a brief naming of the episode rather than a narration, used here to describe an aspect of the linga's significance.

groups.heading: Verse 5 - Kumkum, sandal paste, and the removal of accumulated wrongdoing
groups.body: Lingashtakam here returns to the imagery of ritual anointing, describing the linga as smeared with kumkum and sandal paste and beautifully adorned with a garland of lotuses. The verse states that the linga destroys accumulated sin - papa that has built up over time - continuing the pattern of pairing a physical, sensory description of the linga with a statement of what devotion to it is traditionally held to address, before closing with the familiar line of salutation to Sadashiva.

groups.heading: Verse 6 - Served by hosts of gods and radiant as countless suns
groups.body: The sixth verse of Lingashtakam speaks of the linga as served and worshipped by groups of gods, approached through feeling and devotion rather than through any external requirement. It is described as radiant like the light of a million suns, an image used often in Shiva stotras to convey an intensity of brilliance beyond ordinary comparison. The verse keeps to the established form of Lingashtakam, building a picture through accumulated epithets rather than narrative.

groups.heading: Verse 7 - The eight-petalled seat and the eight forms of poverty
groups.body: This verse of Lingashtakam places the linga upon what is described as an eight-petalled base, and calls it the cause from which all things arise. It also refers to the linga as that which destroys the eight kinds of déficiency or poverty, a traditional listing of various forms of lack. As elsewhere in the text, the verse does not explain the list in detail - it names the idea and moves to the closing salutation that ends every verse of Lingashtakam.

groups.heading: Verse 8 and the closing couplet - Worshipped by Brihaspati and the fruit of recitation
groups.body: The final verse of Lingashtakam describes the linga as worshipped by Brihaspati, the teacher of the gods, and by the best among the gods, offered flowers from the divine gardens, and calls it the supreme reality beyond the beyond. After the eight verses, a closing couplet states that one who recites this meritorious Lingashtakam in the presence of Shiva attains the world of Shiva and rejoices together with him - a traditional statement of fruit (phalashruti) attached to the end of the stotra.

recitation: Lingashtakam is commonly recited during the worship of a Shiva linga, whether at home before a small linga or image, or at a temple where the main deity is installed in linga form. It is heard frequently during Pradosha, the twilight period that falls twice a month and is considered especially suited to Shiva worship, and through the month of Shravan, when many devotees observe fasts and visit Shiva temples. Monday, held as Shiva's day in the week, is another common occasion for reciting Lingashtakam, as is Mahashivratri, the major annual festival dedicated to Shiva, when the text is often chanted repeatedly through the night alongside other Shiva stotras. In temple settings, Lingashtakam is usually recited aloud by a group, sometimes led by a priest, timed to accompany the abhisheka - the ritual bathing of the linga with water, milk, honey and other substances - since several of its verses describe the linga being anointed. At home, people typically recite it once or a small number of times after lighting a lamp, without any fixed count being mandatory; the text itself does not specify a required number of repetitions, only stating what is held to follow from reciting it in Shiva's presence.
tradition: The tradition around Lingashtakam holds it to be a stotra of praise rather than a petition - it does not ask Shiva for anything specific but builds a picture of the linga through repeated description and salutation. The closing couplet states that reciting this Lingashtakam with merit in the presence of Shiva leads to reaching Shiva's world and joy in his company; this is presented as the text's own stated fruit, a common feature of phalashruti verses attached to stotras, and is understood within the devotional framework of Shiva worship rather than as a claim verifiable outside it. Teachers within the Shaiva tradition generally present Lingashtakam as suitable for anyone with devotion to Shiva, without restriction by caste, age or scholarly qualification - a feature noted of many popular Sanskrit stotras meant for wide recitation. It is valued less for philosophical exposition, of which it has little, and more as a vehicle for bhakti, devotional feeling directed at the linga as a form of Shiva.

faq.a: Lingashtakam is a set of eight short verses describing the Shiva linga - its purity, fragrance, the gods and sages who honour it, and a few well-known episodes from Shiva's mythology - each verse ending in the same line of salutation. A closing couplet adds what tradition holds about reciting it.

The author of Lingashtakam is not recorded by name. Like many Sanskrit stotras that have circulated through oral and temple tradition over a long period, it is treated as traditional rather than attributed to a specific, datable poet.

It is commonly recited during Shiva worship, especially on Mondays, during Pradosha, through Shravan month, and on Mahashivratri. It is also chanted in temples alongside the abhisheka, the ritual bathing of the linga, since several verses describe this act of anointing.

faq.q: Do I need a linga at home to recite Lingashtakam?
faq.a: A physical linga is not described in the tradition as a strict requirement for personal recitation. Many people recite Lingashtakam before an image of Shiva, or simply with Shiva in mind, though reciting it in front of an actual linga is the setting the text itself describes and the one most associated with temple practice.

faq.q: Is there a fixed number of times Lingashtakam should be recited?
faq.a: No specific count is given within Lingashtakam itself. The closing couplet speaks of reciting it with merit in Shiva's presence, without stating a number, so people recite it once, a few times, or repeatedly through the night during occasions like Mahashivratri, according to personal or local custom.
